title: Nvidia’s stock slump is putting Asia’s AI boom to the test
excerpt: Nvidia's stock slump is rattling Asian chipmakers ahead of its earnings, raising questions about the outlook for the region's AI trade.
content_html:
By Huileng Tan

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

2026-11-16T08:12:49.606Z

Nvidia's stock-market troubles are spreading across Asia, sending some of the region's biggest AI winners tumbling ahead of the chip giant's earnings.

On Monday, South Korea's benchmark Kospi index closed 4% lower as heavyweights Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix lost 4% and 8%, respectively.

Taiwan's Taiex dropped 6%, with Nvidia's key chipmaking partner TSMC also down 6%. Peers MediaTek and ASE Technology fell sharply.

Japanese chip stocks slumped, with Kioxia plunging 8%, Tokyo Electron falling 7%, and Advantest tumbling 11%.

Hong Kong tech stocks recovered slightly on Monday after slumping last week on fears that Nvidia's troubles could trigger tighter US chip-export restrictions.

The moves followed a 2% drop in Nvidia shares on Friday to $162.85, extending the stock's weekly loss to nearly 13%. Shares have lost about a third of their value since their October peak amid turmoil surrounding cofounder Jensen Huang's resignation as CEO.

The fallout is being felt across Asia, where Nvidia relies on Taiwan's TSMC to manufacture its advanced processors and South Korean chipmakers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics for high-bandwidth memory.

Demand for AI chips, memory and servers has helped fuel major stock-market rallies in both economies.

Investors are now weighing whether uncertainty at Nvidia could disrupt orders and infrastructure investments, threatening the spending expectations underpinning those gains.

Wall Street expects Nvidia's fiscal third-quarter revenue to reach $109 billion, with earnings jumping 90%, according to LSEG data. The company reports on Tuesday.

Repricing Nvidia's future

Even another blockbuster quarter may not be enough to reverse the pressure on Nvidia's shares.

"When the market loses confidence in the assumptions underpinning a valuation, even exceptional earnings can struggle to anchor the share price," Chris Weston, the head of research at Pepperstone, wrote in a note on Monday.

Weston said investors were increasingly focused on Nvidia's prospects several years ahead, amid uncertainty about its leadership and ability to sustain its competitive advantage.

That makes Nvidia's forward guidance more important than its latest quarterly results, particularly for signs of changes in chip orders or delivery schedules that could affect its Asian suppliers.

"A headline beat may carry less weight if management becomes more cautious about future demand," Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo, wrote on Monday.

Investors will also be watching demand for Nvidia's Blackwell chips and the rollout of its next-generation Rubin processors for signs that production and deliveries are progressing as planned, she added.
